tagline: Mountain roads connect conifer forests with the palms of the desert
intro: Palms to Pines links Banning Pass and Palm Desert across 67 miles of mountain and desert country. The Forest Service emphasizes the contrast between desert palms and high-country conifer forests along this National Forest Scenic Byway. Its Banning section offers views toward the San Gorgonio Wilderness; Highway 243 is a two-lane road with curves and switchbacks. Along the Banning Pass section, the view also takes in craggy mountains and the developed valley floor below.

The Banning-to-Idyllwild road was under construction in 1904 and completed as an oiled road in September 1910. The federal government contributed $2,000 because the road was expected to help haul lumber and fight fires. The road became part of the forest highway system in 1927, before its later state designation. Riverside County supervisors named the mountain-to-desert highway Palms to Pines in 1930. The Banning road joined the state highway system as Route 243 in 1970.

From Banning, take Highway 243 up the switchbacks and through forest to Pine Cove and Idyllwild, then continue to Mountain Center. Highway 74 follows Garner Valley, crosses the Santa Rosa Indian Reservation and passes Pinyon Pines. It turns along Deep Canyon and descends beside Carrizo Creek into Palm Desert.

moments.title: Idyllwild
moments.text: Strawberry Creek runs year-round through the high mountain valley occupied by Idyllwild. The town was first known as Strawberry Valley, after the wild fruit growing beside the creek. A toll road from Hemet opened the area to logging and tourism by the 1890s. A sanatorium built in 1901 to treat tuberculosis patients was soon remodeled as a resort. Automobiles later made it a weekend destination for Southern Californians. For years, businesses adopted German-sounding names to present an alpine village, a practice that ended during World War II. Tahquitz Peak and Suicide Rock flank the town.

moments.title: Pinyon Pines
moments.text: Pinyon Pines takes its name from the native pinyon pines in this small valley between the San Jacinto and Santa Rosa mountains. The community sits north of Highway 74 at approximately 4,000 feet. Its beginnings are tied to roadbuilding: Art Nightingale founded it in the 1930s, around the time the Pines to Palms Highway was being built. A mechanic who invested in Pinyon Flats, Nightingale built accommodations for highway workers and the Sugarloaf Cafe, which has since closed.

moments.title: Seven Level Hill
moments.text: Seven Level Hill, a stretch of Highway 74 just south of Palm Desert, supplied the opening encounter in the 1963 comedy It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World. The principal characters meet here after a car accident near mile marker 87.
